nodes.summary: Sets default USAGE and SELECT sequence privileges for the service role on future sequences owned by the migration user.

nodes.summary: Grants the configured table privileges to the service role on existing tables in the schema.

nodes.name: postgresql_grant.microservice-user-sequence
nodes.summary: Grants USAGE and SELECT on existing sequences to the service role.

nodes.name: random_password.m_password
nodes.summary: Generates a 16-character password with special characters for the migration role login credential.

nodes.name: postgresql_role.migration_user

nodes.name: postgresql_grant.microservice-migration-executer
nodes.summary: Grants USAGE and CREATE on the schema to the migration role so it can create and alter objects.

nodes.name: postgresql_grant.microservice-migration-executer-tables
nodes.summary: Grants full DML (INSERT, SELECT, REFERENCES, UPDATE, DELETE) on tables to the migration role.

nodes.name: postgresql_grant.microservice-migration-executor-sequence
nodes.summary: Grants USAGE and SELECT on sequences to the migration role.

tour.title: Project Overview & CI
tour.description: Start here to learn what this repository is: the infrastructure-as-code that provisions and operates the Greenstand treetracker platform across DigitalOcean and AWS. The root README maps the major subsystems, while the pre-commit config and GitHub Actions workflow show the guardrail that keeps every Terraform change formatted and linted before it merges. This is a monorepo of independent stacks, not a single application, so the tour follows the platform's architectural layers rather than a code call graph.

tour.title: Terraform Provisioning Foundations
tour.description: Every stack shares the same pattern: a pinned cloud provider plus an S3-compatible remote state backend. DigitalOcean stacks pin the digitalocean provider and store state in DigitalOcean Spaces buckets, while AWS stacks use the hashicorp/aws provider with real S3. Understanding these provider and backend blocks unlocks how to read every other Terraform directory in the repo.
tour.languageLesson: Terraform separates the provider (which cloud API to talk to) from the backend (where the state file lives). DigitalOcean Spaces is S3-compatible, so an 'S3' backend block points at a Spaces endpoint. State tracks real infrastructure, so plan before apply to preview changes.

tour.title: Compute: DOKS Clusters & Bastion
tour.description: The compute foundation is a set of DigitalOcean Kubernetes (DOKS) clusters, each with dedicated node pools for microservices, cloud-services, and monitoring, all with autoscaling. A hardened bastion host, built from a shared external module, provides controlled SSH access into the private network. Almost every workload later in the tour runs on top of these clusters.

tour.title: Managed Postgres Database
tour.description: Building on the compute layer, the production data tier is a DigitalOcean managed PostgreSQL cluster with a read replica, firewall rules that restrict access to tagged resources and the bastion, and several application databases (treetracker, data_pipeline, ckan, world_bank_backup). This single cluster (the highest fan-in resource after the schema module) backs nearly every service in the platform.

tour.title: Database Schemas & Least-Privilege Grants
tour.description: The database-grants stack is the most reused module in the repo. The prod root module fans out to fifteen per-microservice schemas, each instantiated through the reusable microservice_schema module, which creates a schema plus three roles: a service role for runtime, a migration role that owns objects, and shared read-only access. A separate read-only reporting role then gets SELECT across every schema. This is the platform's model for tenant isolation and least privilege inside one shared database.
tour.languageLesson: PostgreSQL default privileges (ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES) grant access to objects that do not exist yet. The migration role owns tables so future tables it creates automatically become readable by the service and read-only roles, which is how least-privilege survives ongoing migrations.

tour.title: Kubernetes Secrets: Sealed Secrets
tour.description: Before deploying workloads, the platform needs a safe way to keep credentials in git. Bitnami Sealed Secrets solves this: kubeseal encrypts a normal Kubernetes Secret into a SealedSecret that only the in-cluster controller can decrypt, so it is safe to commit. The interactive create-secret.sh helper (a high fan-in script) is the entry point operators use, and specialized wrappers exist for things like RabbitMQ connection strings.
tour.languageLesson: A SealedSecret is asymmetric-encrypted: the public sealing key encrypts, only the cluster controller's private key decrypts. This lets encrypted secrets live in version control while the plaintext never does.

tour.title: API Gateway: Ambassador Ingress
tour.description: Ambassador is the single ingress that fronts every backend service on the cluster. It is installed via an Ansible playbook and configured with Mapping custom resources that route URL prefixes to in-cluster services. Terraform then provisions the DigitalOcean DNS records and load balancer wiring. Every later workload exposes itself through an Ambassador Mapping like the one shown here.

tour.title: Identity: Keycloak
tour.description: Keycloak is the platform's identity provider. A multi-stage Dockerfile bakes the custom treetracker theme onto the official Keycloak image, and the Kubernetes base wires the deployment to Postgres using credentials from a Secret, exposed at /keycloak through Ambassador. Kustomize overlays layer per-environment config on the shared base and, critically, pull production credentials from the SealedSecret pattern of Step 6.
tour.languageLesson: Kustomize uses a shared base plus per-environment overlays. An overlay references the base, adds resources (like a SealedSecret), and applies strategic-merge patches to inject environment-specific values without duplicating the whole manifest.

tour.title: Messaging: RabbitMQ
tour.description: Asynchronous communication between services runs on RabbitMQ, deployed as a 3-replica RabbitmqCluster custom resource via the RabbitMQ Operator. The manifests follow the same Kustomize base-plus-overlays structure as Keycloak, isolated in its own namespace, with a PodMonitor that feeds metrics to Prometheus (Step 12). Per-environment deploy scripts switch kubectl context and apply the right overlay.

tour.title: Workflow & Data Platform
tour.description: Two higher-level platforms sit on the cluster and database. Airflow, installed by an Ansible-driven Helm chart, orchestrates scheduled data workflows and exposes a control panel through Ambassador. Apache Solr (deployed with the Solr Operator) and CKAN provide search and the open-data portal; CKAN's Helm values wire it to the managed Postgres from Step 4 and to Solr for indexing.

tour.title: Static Web Apps & CDN
tour.description: The user-facing front-ends are static sites hosted on AWS. The web-apps Terraform provisions S3-backed static websites (web map, wallet) across dev, staging, and prod using a shared Greenstand static-website module, and cdn-images-api fronts the treetracker image store with a CloudFront distribution. This is the only major layer that lives entirely on AWS rather than DigitalOcean.

tour.title: Observability: Metrics, Logs & Tracing
tour.description: The platform is observed through a Prometheus/Grafana metrics stack, Loki for logs, and Jaeger for distributed tracing, all installed via Ansible playbooks and exposed through Ambassador mappings. The PodMonitors and ServiceMonitors seen in earlier steps (like RabbitMQ's) feed this stack, closing the loop between deployed workloads and their telemetry.

tour.title: Operational Tooling & Backups
tour.description: The tour closes with the day-to-day operations layer. The scripts guide documents how operators authenticate to each DOKS cluster with doctl and helm, a Python utility lists deployments across namespaces for at-a-glance cluster state, and a dedicated AWS S3 bucket stores production database backups. Together these tie the whole platform back to the people who run it.
